t: LeetCode 1670 — Design Front Middle Back Queue: Two Balanced Deques Around the Middle
o:
We must support six operations - push/pop at the front, the middle, and the back - where the middle is defined precisely: pushing inserts at index floor(n/2) (pushing 6 into [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] gives [1, 2, 6, 3, 4, 5]) and popping removes index floor((n-1)/2) (popping [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] returns 3, the frontmost of the two middles). Pops on an empty queue return -1.

Example 1 exercises everything: pushFront(1), pushBack(2), pushMiddle(3), pushMiddle(4) build [1, 4, 3, 2]; then the pops return 1, 3, 4, 2 and finally -1 from the emptied queue.

At most 1000 calls are made, so even an O(n)-per-operation dynamic array passes comfortably - but the interesting engineering target is true O(1) per operation, achievable by splitting the queue into two balanced halves or by walking a linked list with a mid pointer.
k: The insertion middle index is floor(n/2) and the removal middle index is floor((n-1)/2) - mixing these up breaks the frontmost-middle tie-break.

Split the queue into a left half holding the first ceil(n/2) elements and a right half with the rest; then every operation becomes end-only work on two deques plus an occasional one-element rebalance.
Because the operation count is capped at 1000, an O(n) dynamic-array solution is a legitimate baseline before optimizing.

a.n: Approach 1: Dynamic Array with Interior Insert/Erase
a.i: Keep one resizable array. Pushes and pops at the ends are cheap; middle operations splice at the computed index. This is the most direct translation of the statement and is perfectly adequate at this input scale.
s: Store all elements in a dynamic array.
pushFront inserts at index 0; pushBack appends.
popMiddle erases index floor((size-1)/2); popFront erases index 0; popBack erases the last index.
Every pop returns -1 immediately when the array is empty.
a.t: O(n) per middle operation — splicing at an interior index shifts up to n elements; end operations are O(1)
a.sp: O(n) — one slot per stored element

a.i: Hold the first ceil(n/2) elements in a left deque and the remainder in a right deque. Front operations touch the left end of left, back operations touch the right end of right, and the middle is always an endpoint: pushMiddle appends to left, popMiddle removes the tail of left. Whenever the halves drift out of balance (sizes must satisfy |left| = |right| or |left| = |right| + 1), move a single element across the boundary.
s: Maintain deques left and right with |left| equal to |right| or |right| + 1.
pushFront prepends to left; pushBack appends to right; both rebalance afterwards.
pushMiddle: if left is currently the larger half, move its tail to the front of right, then append the value to left.
popMiddle removes and returns the tail of left; popBack falls back to the tail of left when right is empty.
Rebalance after every size change by shifting one element toward the smaller half.
a.t: O(1) per operation — each call touches a constant number of deque ends
a.sp: O(n) — the two deques together store all elements

w:
Lead with the array version to lock down the middle-index conventions, then upgrade to the balanced deques. A doubly linked list with a mid pointer achieves the same O(1) bounds and makes a good follow-up exercise.
Pitfalls: using floor(n/2) as the removal index (violates the frontmost-middle rule), forgetting to rebalance after popMiddle, and mishandling popBack when a single element remains (right is empty but left is not).
Follow-ups: generalize to insert/delete at any rank (leads to balanced BSTs / order-statistic trees), or support peekMiddle without removal.
